parole.significato: A well-muscled, short-legged breed of hunting terrier.
parole.testo: From Czech český (“Czech”); the breed was created by a Czech breeder, František Horák, in 1948, as a cross between a Sealyham terrier and a Scottish terrier, to create a terrier suitable for hunting in the forests of Bohemia.

parole.testo: From Czech Dvořák, from Old Czech dvořák (“attendant, tenant farmer”), equivalent to dvůr (“court, courtyard, estate, farm”) + -ák (“-er, -an: forming related nouns”). The keyboard is named after the American inventor August Dvorak.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or characteristic of Antonín Dvořák (1841–1904), Czech composer of Romantic music.
parole.testo: From Dvorak + -ian, from Czech Dvořák.

parole.significato: A traditional variety of thick, soft noodles or dumplings found in many Central and Eastern European cuisines.
parole.testo: From Czech halušky, Polish hałuski, Slovak halušky, Ukrainian галу́шки (halúšky).

parole.significato: Czech or Slovak cabbage rolls.
parole.testo: From Czech holubky and Slovak holubky. Doublet of golabki.

parole.significato: A kalach with sausage filling.

parole.significato: A type of pastry that holds a portion of fruit or cheese, surrounded by a puffy cushion of supple dough.
parole.testo: From Czech and Slovak koláč, from Proto-Slavic *kolačь.

parole.significato: A pastry consisting of a filling (typically fruit or cheese) inside a bread roll, popular in the United States.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Czech koláče and Slovak koláče, plural of koláč. Doublet of kalach and kolach.

parole.significato: The currency of the former Czechoslovakia, divided into 100 hellers.
parole.testo: From Czech and Slovak koruna; cognate with krone and German Krone. Doublet of corona, crown, korona, krona, króna, and krone.

parole.significato: A Czech prefab
parole.testo: From Czech panelák.

parole.significato: Czech or Slovak pierogi.
parole.testo: From Czech pirohy and Slovak pirohy. Doublet of pierogi (from Polish), pirogi (from Russian), and pyrohy (from Ukrainian).

parole.significato: An intelligent mechanical being designed to look like a human or other creature, and usually made from metal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Czech robot, from robota (“drudgery, servitude”). Coined in the 1920 science-fiction play R.U.R. by Karel Čapek after having been suggested to him by his brother Josef. parole.significato: Synonym.

parole.testo: From the Czech tečka (“dot, point, spot; period, full stop; tittle; dot (diacritic), tečka”).
